body_markdown:
Today’s subject takes us back to spring. That beautiful time when winter winds have abated, and the car shows start up once more in the cooler parts of the States. *(It’s a fond memory as many of us are looking at the first rounds of snow this year. —Ed.)* The Saturday before Mother’s Day, there are two very good car shows a convenient drive away, where I can drive up and back home the same day and not have to deal with overnight accommodations. The Alpha, Illinois show, and the Loafers show in Hannibal, Missouri.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


I have been to both in the past; in fact, the[1969 Mustang Grande I wrote up a while back](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1969-ford-mustang-grande-equine-luxury/) was one from the Loafers show, and last year I saw a fantastic light blue 1966 Chrysler New Yorker four-door hardtop there that I still need to do a column on. So, which show? I mean, technically I could have done both, but that would have been way too much driving for one day.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Fortunately, I was able to decide when my friend Jessica Grissom said she wouldn’t mind going to the Alpha show. Plus, it was a much easier drive than Hannibal. So that’s where we went. And today’s subject, while not the *only* really cool car in attendance (there was a tan ’75-’76 Gremlin X and a mint green ’59 Edsel too), this Trans Am was my favorite.


Thomas Klockau


What you see before you today is a Lucerne Blue example of one of a mere 2116 1971 Trans Ams built. And what really drew me in was the blue paint with the matching blue interior. I *loved* the blue interior—so much better than a boring black interior. That and the factory-correct “honeycomb” wheels had me smitten—even though it wasn’t a Cadillac, Imperial, or Lincoln Continental.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As I was going through my automotive library taking notes for this column, I was surprised so few ’71 Trans Ams were made. Some of this is due to the UAW strike from September to November of 1970, when 1971 model-year cars would have otherwise been getting built. The Trans Am’s popularity rose as the decade went on, though, and the fantastic movie “Smokey and the Bandit” seriously increased Trans Am interest, to the point that Trans Ams outsold the lesser trims.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Even by 1975, over 27,000 Trans Ams were sold—though this can likely be at least partially explained by the demise of the traditional ‘big’ Mustang for the Mustang II in autumn ’73 and the disappearance of the AMC Javelin/Javelin AMX after the ’74 model year.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Of course, the Trans Am was the priciest and fastest Firebird. All Trans Ams got Rally gauges (with a tachometer, of course, included), honeycomb wheels (though the Pontiac Rally wheels could also be specified), color-keyed dual sport mirrors, front and rear spoilers, special striping with a “Firebird” bird up front (a much smaller version than that which would be seen on mid-’70s and later models), and a “shaker” reverse hood scoop.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Said scoop was a legitimate cold air intake, not just “for looks,” and was throttle-activated. But of course the big deal was the Trans Am engine: the LS5 455 CID V-8. It breathed through a four-barrel carb, had an 8.4:1 compression ratio, and delivered 335 hp at 4600 rpm.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


What cost, speed and style? $4594 in 1971. Curb weight was 3578 lbs. Of course, you could get the 455 in lesser Firebirds, but not all the extra functional and appearance items of the Trans Am.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


In 1971,[a base Firebird](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-1970-81-pontiac-firebird-buyers-guide/) , complete with dog dish hubcaps and few frills, retailed for $3047. Available 1971 colors included Carousel Red, Orbit Orange, Tropical Lime, Sandalwood, Aquarius Green, Goldenrod Yellow, and Rosewood.


Pontiac


The luxury-oriented Esprit, which added nicer seats and door panels with simulated woodgrain trim, went for $3416, while the sporty but not quite Trans Am-level Formula went for $3445.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


But this was Detroit in the ’70s, so even the tonier models had all sorts of options you could get, and of course goodies like factory A/C, an eight-track player, and other stuff would bump the price further. But a lot of items optional on the other Firebirds came standard on the Trans Am, and some items it had couldn’t be had on the other Firebird models at all.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


But that $4500 was quite a bit for a ponycar, even a really nice one. You could instead get a giant, luxurious Olds Delta 88 Royale convertible that same year for $4325! But of course that was a completely different kind of car. But the price likely kept production down on ’71 Trans Ams, with the base ‘Bird $1500 cheaper.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Fun fact: of the 2116 1971 Trans Ams produced, 1231 of them had automatics. But our featured car had the four-speed stick shift. As the ’71 Pontiac performance cars brochure said, “It’s hard to stay calm about a car like Pontiac’s Firebird Trans Am.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“Because we got it all together for this one. Everything that makes an enthusiast enthusiastic is standard equipment. Start with the most obvious. A front air dam. Side air extractors. A spoiler at each wheel. They all work. Providing 50 lbs. of downward pressure, both front and rear.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“The shaker hood works, too. When you punch the throttle, a rear-facing inlet door allows air to be rammed directly to the Quadra-Jet carb.


Thomas Klockau


“It is, frankly, not for every driver. But if you want to experience the ultimate—the state of the art—in enthusiast driving, there is no other choice. Firebird Trans Am. Pure Pontiac!”


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And it sure was pretty in blue! So while I may have missed some neat cars in Hannibal, this Trans Am made me regret nothing! And the late lunch we had at City Limits in Viola after the show was excellent, too. Great burger baskets.


Pontiac


I can’t wait for car season next spring! Until next time: always tip your bartender, and Brougham on! Even if your favorite car was a ponycar.
